questions.clue: A numerical outcome whose possible values form a countable set.
questions.explanation: The possible values can be listed, even if the list has no end.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 356, Random variable

questions.clue: A numerical outcome that can take any value in an interval, such as a measurement before rounding.
questions.explanation: A density assigns probabilities to intervals of possible values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 102, Continuous variable

questions.clue: A function that gives the probability of each individual value of a discrete variable.
questions.explanation: Its values are point probabilities, and they sum to one.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 338, Probability distribution

questions.clue: A nonnegative function whose area over an interval gives its probability.
questions.explanation: Integrating the density over a range gives the chance of landing in that range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 338, Probability density

questions.clue: A function giving the chance that a random variable does not exceed a specified value.
questions.explanation: For each cutoff x, it returns the probability that X is at most x.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 117, Cumulative distribution function. Uses the at-most convention from MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: A variable coded 1 when an event occurs and 0 otherwise.
questions.explanation: Its numerical value records whether the specified event happened.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 216, Indicator variable

questions.clue: Record 1 if a single coin toss is heads and 0 otherwise. What is the model for the recorded value?
questions.explanation: A single binary trial with fixed success probability follows a Bernoulli model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 42, Bernoulli distribution

questions.clue: Count heads in 20 independent tosses of the same coin, with a fixed chance of heads.
questions.explanation: This counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with a common success chance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution

questions.clue: Calls arrive one at a time, independently, at a steady rate. What models the hourly count?
questions.explanation: The event count in a fixed period of a homogeneous Poisson process has a Poisson distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson distribution

questions.clue: Toss the same coin independently until the first head. Record the total tosses.
questions.explanation: The geometric model describes trials to the first success under independent trials with constant success probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 186, Geometric distribution
questions.convention: Counts the successful trial, so the smallest value is 1.

questions.clue: Draw five cards from a shuffled deck without replacement. Count the aces.
questions.explanation: Sampling without replacement from a fixed population leads to a hypergeometric count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 211, Hypergeometric distribution

questions.clue: A wheel’s landing angle has equal probability in every arc of the same length.
questions.explanation: A continuous uniform model has constant density on its range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 441, Uniform distribution

questions.clue:
Σₓ x · P(X = x)
for a discrete X
questions.explanation: The expected value weights each possible outcome by its probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 156, Expected value

questions.clue:
E[(X − μ)²]
where μ = E[X]
questions.explanation: Variance measures the expected squared distance from the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance

questions.clue:
σ / √n
for n independent draws with standard deviation σ
questions.explanation: Averaging n independent draws divides their standard deviation by the square root of n.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue:
X / n
where X is the number of successes in n trials
questions.explanation: The proportion is the observed number of successes divided by the total trial count.
questions.reference: UC Berkeley STAT 2, Fall 2024, Module 7, sample percentage: https://stat2.berkeley.edu/fall-2024/#module-7-sampling-from-a-population-weeks-11-12

questions.clue:
(x − μ) / σ
where μ and σ are population values
questions.explanation: This gives the number of population standard deviations from the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard scores

questions.clue:
F(b) − F(a)
for a cumulative distribution function F and a < b
questions.explanation: Subtracting the cumulative probabilities gives P(a < X ≤ b).
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b, Cumulative Distribution Function: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: The probability distribution of a statistic across repeated samples of a fixed size.
questions.explanation: The variable here is the statistic, such as a sample mean, rather than an individual measurement.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: Differences in a statistic that arise when equal-sized random samples are drawn from one population.
questions.explanation: Different random samples can give different values of the same statistic.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling variation

questions.clue: Learning the outcomes of earlier draws leaves the probability law for the next draw unchanged.
questions.explanation: Earlier outcomes carry no information about the next draw when the draws are independent.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 3, §6: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class03-prep.pdf

questions.clue: What theorem gives a normal limit for standardized means of independent draws from one finite-variance population?
questions.explanation: This theorem concerns the shape of the standardized sampling distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: As independent draws accumulate, their average approaches the population mean, when the mean exists.
questions.explanation: The law concerns the location of the average as the sample grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 244, Law of large numbers

questions.clue: Using a bell-shaped model for averages of large independent samples from a skewed, finite-variance population.
questions.explanation: For large samples, the central limit theorem makes the normal model a useful approximation for the sample mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation. Sample mean case in MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: Measure the wait from now until the first arrival of a constant-rate Poisson process.
questions.explanation: The continuous wait to the next event is exponential under this process.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution

questions.clue: Measure the time to the fourth arrival in a constant-rate Poisson process.
questions.explanation: A sum of four independent exponential waits with a common rate has a gamma distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 179, Gamma distribution
questions.convention: Shape 4, with rate equal to the arrival rate. The scale is its reciprocal.

questions.clue: A positive variable becomes normally distributed after taking its natural logarithm.
questions.explanation: The normality applies to the log of the variable itself.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 259, Lognormal distribution

questions.clue: Gaussian sensor readings are rescaled to have mean zero and variance one. What is the resulting distribution?
questions.explanation: A normal distribution with mean zero and variance one is standard normal.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard normal variable

questions.clue: Toss the same coin independently. Count tails before the fourth head.
questions.explanation: For independent tosses with a fixed success probability, the failure count before a fixed number of successes follows a negative binomial model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 298, Negative binomial distribution
questions.convention: Counts failures before the fixed success count.

questions.clue: A probability p varies across machines with density proportional to p(1 − p) for 0 < p < 1.
questions.explanation: The density is a beta model with both shape parameters equal to two.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 43, Beta distribution

questions.clue:
√[(N − n) / (N − 1)]
for n draws without replacement from N > 1 units
questions.explanation: This factor shrinks the standard error relative to drawing with replacement.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 166, Finite population correction
questions.convention: Here the population variance uses denominator N and the correction multiplies the standard error.

questions.clue: E[(X − μₓ)(Y − μᵧ)]
questions.explanation: Covariance averages the product of the centered variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 110, Covariance

questions.clue:
Cov(X, Y) / (σₓσᵧ)
with positive standard deviations
questions.explanation: Pearson correlation is covariance scaled by the two standard deviations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 107, Correlation coefficient

questions.clue:
Σᵧ P(X = x, Y = y)
for discrete X and Y
questions.explanation: Summing over Y gives the probability that X takes the specified value.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 267, Marginal distribution

questions.clue:
P(X = x, Y = y) / P(Y = y)
with a positive denominator
questions.explanation: The ratio gives the chance that X equals x within the group where Y equals y.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 98, Conditional distribution

questions.clue:
1 − F(t)
where F(t) = P(T ≤ t) and T is time to an event
questions.explanation: The survival function gives the chance that the event happens after t.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 423, Survival function

questions.clue: Independent readings are normally distributed. What describes the sample mean’s distribution, even with only four readings?
questions.explanation: The mean of independent normal readings is itself exactly normal.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 26, §26.1, Sums of Independent Normal Random Variables: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson26

questions.clue: A computer picks eight distinct employees so that every possible group of eight has the same chance.
questions.explanation: A simple random sample without replacement makes all size-eight subsets equally likely.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 394, Simple random sampling

questions.clue:
E[exp(tX)]
where this expectation exists around t = 0
questions.explanation: Taking the expectation of the exponential gives the moment generating function.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 282, Moment generating function

questions.clue:
Var(X) + Var(Y)
for independent X and Y with finite variances
questions.explanation: Independence makes the covariance zero, so the variances add.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 7b, Covariance and Correlation, variance of a sum: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class07-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: A fixed numerical feature of the entire population, such as its true proportion of left-handed people.
questions.explanation: A population parameter describes the population supplying the sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 317, Parameter

questions.clue: A numerical summary calculated from sample data alone, without unknown population quantities.
questions.explanation: A statistic is a function of the observed sample, such as its mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 411, Statistic

questions.clue: A cutoff at or below which a specified percentage of a continuous distribution falls.
questions.explanation: A percentile translates a cumulative percentage into a value on the measurement scale.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Percentile

questions.clue: The list used to identify the units from which a sample can actually be drawn.
questions.explanation: The frame is the operational list, which can differ from the target population.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 100, Lesson 2, Sampling Methods: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson02

questions.clue: A fair ten-sided die has one face for each integer from 0 to 9. What models the number shown?
questions.explanation: Each of the ten discrete results has the same probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 441, Uniform distribution

questions.clue: A library splits its branches by region and randomly samples branches from every region.
questions.explanation: The regions are strata, and every stratum contributes to the sample.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 100, Lesson 2, Sampling Methods: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson02

questions.clue: A library randomly selects two branches and surveys every staff member at both.
questions.explanation: The branches are clusters, and all people in selected clusters are included.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 87, Cluster sampling

questions.clue: From a list, a pollster picks a random start among the first ten entries, then takes every tenth entry.
questions.explanation: A random start followed by a fixed interval defines systematic sampling.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 100, Lesson 2, Sampling Methods: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson02

questions.clue:
aE[X] + b
when a and b are constants and Y = aX + b
questions.explanation: Multiplying values multiplies their mean, and adding a fixed amount shifts it.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Problem Set 4 Solutions, affine transformations: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_pset04_sol.pdf

questions.clue:
a² Var(X)
for Y = aX + b, with a and b fixed
questions.explanation: Adding b shifts the center; multiplying by a scales the variance by a squared.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Problem Set 4 Solutions, affine transformations: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_pset04_sol.pdf

questions.clue:
np
for X counting successes in n independent trials with fixed success chance p
choices: Standard deviation of a binomial count
questions.explanation: The count is a sum of n variables whose individual means are p.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution

questions.clue:
p(1 − p)
for X equal to 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise
questions.explanation: The variance of a single indicator is p times one minus p.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 42, Bernoulli distribution

questions.clue: One probability model describes two random variables together, including how their values occur in combination.
questions.explanation: The joint distribution retains information about the relationship between the variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 229, Joint distribution

questions.clue: In a distribution with a finite third moment, the average cubed deviation from the mean is positive.
questions.explanation: Cubing retains the sign of deviations, so large positive deviations can dominate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 397, Skewness

questions.clue: The standardized fourth central moment minus the corresponding value for a normal distribution.
questions.explanation: A normal distribution has kurtosis of three, so its excess kurtosis is zero.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 239, Kurtosis
questions.convention: Excess kurtosis uses normal as the zero reference.

questions.clue: Repeatedly drawing same-size samples with replacement from the observed data to approximate a statistic’s sampling behavior.
questions.explanation: The nonparametric bootstrap uses the observed sample as a stand-in for the population.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bootstrap

questions.clue: For every fixed positive tolerance, the chance of an estimator missing its limit by more than that tolerance tends to zero.
questions.explanation: This mode of convergence controls the probability of deviations from the limit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 104, Convergence in probability

questions.clue: What inequality bounds tails for any distribution with finite variance using only distance from the mean in standard deviation units?
questions.explanation: The upper bound for being at least k standard deviations away is 1/k², with positive variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 77, Chebyshev’s inequality

questions.clue: Forty independent voters each pick one of three candidates with fixed probabilities. Model the three counts jointly.
questions.explanation: A multinomial model counts several possible categories across a fixed number of independent trials.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 290, Multinomial distribution

questions.clue: A researcher adds the squares of four independent standard normal values.
questions.explanation: The sum of four independent squared standard normal variables has four chi-squared degrees of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 79, Chi-squared distribution

questions.clue: A lab divides one standard normal reading by another independent standard normal reading.
questions.explanation: The ratio of independent standard normal variables follows the standard Cauchy model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Cauchy distribution Ratio example in University of Minnesota STAT 3701, Statistical Models, Part II: https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/3701/notes/models2.html

questions.clue: A newly started machine has a constant failure rate, and its time to failure is continuous.
questions.explanation: A constant hazard in continuous time leads to an exponential lifetime.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution

questions.clue: As many independent fair-coin tosses accumulate, the proportion of heads stays close to one half with high probability.
questions.explanation: For indicators of heads, the sample mean is the head proportion, and its target is one half.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 244, Law of large numbers

questions.clue: Repair times are right-skewed. For repeated groups of 200 independent repairs, standardized average times have a bell-shaped distribution. Which theorem explains this?
questions.explanation: Independent draws with finite positive variance produce a normal limiting shape after standardization.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue:
exp(−λ) λᵏ / k!
for counts k = 0, 1, 2, …
questions.explanation: The Poisson count law uses a positive expected count λ.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson distribution

questions.clue:
λ exp(−λx)
for x ≥ 0 and λ > 0
questions.explanation: The exponential density decays from λ at rate λ.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution
questions.convention: λ is the rate, with mean 1/λ.

questions.clue:
np(1 − p)
for a count X from n independent binary trials with success chance p
questions.explanation: The count sums n independent indicators, each with variance p times one minus p.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution

questions.clue:
√[p(1 − p) / n]
for n independent trials with true success chance p
choices: Standard deviation of a binary outcome
Standard error of the success count
questions.explanation: The spread of the sample proportion is the spread of its count divided by n.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 500, Lesson 4, §4.2, Sampling Distribution of the Sample Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/Lesson04

questions.clue: E[X⁴], when finite
questions.explanation: A raw moment uses powers of X itself, without centering.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 282, Moments

questions.clue: E[(X − E[X])²]
questions.explanation: A central moment uses deviations around the mean; the second one equals variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 282, Moments

questions.clue: Their joint probability can be written as the product of the two marginal probabilities for every pair of sets.
questions.explanation: Independence requires the factorization for every pair of events defined by the variables.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 7a, Joint Distributions and Independence: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class07-prep-a_pdf/

questions.clue: What describes two variables with finite positive variances when their centered product has expectation zero?
questions.explanation: Zero covariance gives zero Pearson correlation, even if dependence remains.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 107, Correlation coefficient

questions.clue: A bell curve approximates P̂ from independent binary draws when expected success and failure counts are both large.
questions.explanation: A sample proportion is an average of binary indicators; its large-sample shape is approximately normal.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 500, Lesson 4, §4.2, Sampling Distribution of the Sample Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/Lesson04

questions.clue: When using a continuous approximation for an integer count, move an inclusive upper integer cutoff up by one half.
questions.explanation: The half-unit change includes the whole bar for the last qualifying integer.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation See the half-unit correction in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 28: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson28

questions.clue: Divide a standard normal value by √(V/8), where V is independent chi-squared with eight degrees of freedom.
questions.explanation: This ratio follows Student’s t with degrees of freedom inherited from the chi-squared term.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Student’s t-distribution Ratio definition in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 26, §26.4: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson26

questions.clue: A factory checks thousands of independent parts, each with a tiny defect probability. Which model can approximate the defect count using its mean alone?
questions.explanation: A binomial count with many trials and small success probability can be approximated by a Poisson count.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 12, The Poisson Distribution: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson12

questions.clue: Averages of independent Cauchy observations remain Cauchy. Which usual central-limit condition fails?
questions.explanation: The Cauchy distribution has no finite variance, so the elementary normal limit theorem does not apply.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Cauchy distribution

questions.clue: A sensor repeats the same reading 500 times. Which issue defeats an independent-draw central limit argument?
questions.explanation: Copying one observation creates perfectly dependent values, not 500 independent observations.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b, Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue:
√n · (X̄ − μ) / σ
for an independent sample with common mean μ and positive finite SD σ
questions.explanation: Subtract the population mean and divide by the standard error of the sample mean.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b, Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue:
σ² / n
for n independent draws from one distribution with variance σ²
questions.explanation: The variance of the sum is nσ², and scaling by 1/n divides variance by n².
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 24, Several Independent Random Variables: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson24

questions.clue: Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y)
questions.explanation: Dependence can add or subtract from variance through the covariance term.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 7b, Covariance and Correlation: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class07-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue:
dF(x)/dx
for a differentiable cumulative distribution function F
questions.explanation: The derivative of the CDF gives the density where the derivative exists.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b, Continuous Random Variables: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue:
P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] / a
for nonnegative X with finite mean and a > 0
questions.explanation: Nonnegative values above a contribute at least a times their probability to the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 270, Markov inequality

questions.clue:
N(nμ, nσ²)
for the total of many independent draws from one nonnormal population
questions.explanation: Adding n observations scales the mean and variance by n, and the central limit theorem supplies the shape.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b, Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/
questions.convention: N(mean, variance). Population mean μ and finite positive variance σ².
